clue.text: Go to rear of theatre and play second fiddle

definitions.meaning: literally, to move to a seat at the back of the auditorium
to accept a subordinate role and let others lead

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means accepting a lesser role, and taken literally it means sitting further back in a theatre.

clue.text: Order to sailor to exercise, aiming to improve with this?

parts.note: tar is a traditional word for a sailor
to get practice is to exercise a skill

explanation.surface: An instruction to a seaman to train, with the aim of getting better.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Order to sailor to exercise' as the command 'Tar, get practice!'
explanation.definitionFit: Shooting at a target over and over is how one gets better at aiming.

clue.text: Make senseless goal within Asian sport

indicators.note: within means the goal word sits inside the knockout letters

parts.note: KO, a knockout, leaves someone unconscious
an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: A punch knocks a player out during an Asian game.
explanation.definitionFit: Kendo is the Japanese martial art of fencing with bamboo swords.

clue.text: Expressed regret in journal, in article ready to go

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

indicators.note: in means the journal word goes inside the article and readiness words

parts.note: poised means ready to act
a log is a daily record or journal

explanation.surface: A newspaper writer says sorry in print, in a piece ready to run.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' is only a link; the second is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To apologise is to say sorry, which is expressing regret.

clue.text: Sign showing gold mace, say

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
mace is a spice made from nutmeg husks; 'say' marks it as an example

explanation.surface: A golden ceremonial mace is a symbol of office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mace' suggests the ceremonial staff; here it is the spice.
explanation.definitionFit: An auspice is an omen or portent, a sign read for the future.

clue.text: African people knows about no rising

indicators.note: about means the knowing word goes around the reversed refusal

parts.note: ken is a Scots verb meaning to know

indicators.note: rising in a down clue means reading the word upwards, so backwards

parts.note: nay is an old word for no

explanation.surface: An African community understands that refusals are going up.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'rising' reads a word from bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenyans are the citizens of Kenya in East Africa.

clue.text: German's real contribution to speech therapy

indicators.note: contribution to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A German makes a real contribution to helping people speak.
explanation.definitionFit: Echt is the German word for genuine or authentic, also borrowed into English.

clue.text: Dramatizer ignoring first change in verse form

indicators.note: change says the remaining letters are to be rearranged
ignoring first means dropping the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A playwright skips the opening and alters a poem's structure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignoring first' drops D, leaving RAMATIZER, which 'change' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Terza rima is the interlocking three-line rhyme scheme Dante used in the Divine Comedy.

clue.text: Given to thieving, like Pooh after honey?

definitions.meaning: Winnie-the-Pooh's paws would be gummy after eating from the honey pot

explanation.definitionFit: Someone with sticky fingers lets things stick to their hands, so steals; honey literally leaves paws sticky.

clue.text: Little boy to perform piece of music

parts.note: Ron is a short form of the boy's name Ronald
to do is to perform an action

explanation.surface: A young lad is asked to play a musical piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondo is a musical form in which a main theme keeps returning between contrasting episodes.

clue.text: For general education, a preparatory school?

definitions.text: For general education, a preparatory school?

parts.words: For general education, a preparatory school?
parts.note: read 'general' as the military rank: the place that prepares officers who may become generals

explanation.walkthrough: SANDHURST is the Royal Military Academy in England, where British Army officers are trained; the clue pretends to be about a prep school for broad schooling.
explanation.definitionFit: The British officer-training academy is in effect the school where future army generals are first prepared.

clue.text: English getting rich, holding on and saving money

indicators.note: holding means the funny word keeps the other inside it

parts.note: rich in the sense of highly amusing, as in 'that's rich'
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Englishman who grows wealthy by keeping hold of his cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rich' looks like wealth, which suits 'saving money'; it means laughable instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Economical describes thrifty behaviour that avoids spending and so keeps money in hand.

clue.text: Unlike minister, starts to like argument in cabinet

indicators.note: starts to signals taking the opening letter of each of the next four words

explanation.surface: A politician is starting to enjoy debates in the cabinet room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minister' looks political, but here it is a minister of religion: laic means of the laity, not clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: Laic means belonging to the lay people rather than the clergy, so a church minister is the opposite.

clue.text: Why things go wrong in potato salad

parts.note: murphy is a slang word for a potato
slaw is short for coleslaw, a cabbage salad

explanation.surface: Potato salad is to blame when everything goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Murphy as slang for potato comes from the Irish surname, associated with the potato.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying that anything that can go wrong will go wrong is a humorous explanation for mishaps.

clue.text: Slow to react in predicament I have

parts.note: a pass is a difficult state of affairs, as in 'things have come to a pretty pass'
contracted to I've

explanation.surface: Someone admits to being in a fix and slow to respond.
explanation.definitionFit: Passive describes someone inert who accepts things without responding or acting.

clue.text: Where performers barely finish their acts

definitions.text: Where performers barely finish their acts

parts.words: Where performers barely finish their acts
parts.note: barely read as 'bare', naked: dancers end their routines unclothed

explanation.definitionFit: At this kind of venue the dancers remove clothing and end their routines naked.

clue.text: Med island I left, offered a university place, in smart fashion

indicators.note: offered a place means the following letters are given room inside the remaining word
left means the named letter has departed from the island's name

parts.note: Sicily is an island in the Mediterranean
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A student from Sicily leaves home, having been offered a place at a university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' takes I from SICILY to leave SCILY; 'offered' (a place) sets A and U inside it, after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Saucily means cheekily and pertly, and smart can mean impudent or cheeky, as in a smart answer.

clue.text: Still lacking a successor, from what we hear

indicators.note: from what we hear signals that a word pronounced the same way is needed

parts.note: having no heir to inherit

explanation.surface: A monarch is still childless, so rumour goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like an adverb meaning 'yet'; it is the adjective meaning calm, with no wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Still air has no breeze or movement, so a calm windless day can be called still.

clue.text: After Lister's reform, theatre finally becoming this

definitions.text: After Lister's reform, theatre finally becoming this

indicators.note: reform means the name's letters are formed again in a new order

parts.note: the possessive 's is not used, leaving the surgeon's name

indicators.note: finally signals taking the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: After Joseph Lister's reforms of surgery, operating theatres became free of germs.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Lister pioneered antiseptic surgery, so the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lister's antiseptic methods made operating theatres free of germs, which is what sterile means.

clue.text: Top women bribe queen

parts.note: a sop is something given to pacify or buy someone off
a rani is an Indian queen

explanation.surface: Leading ladies pay off a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top women' means the singers with the highest voices, not leading women.
explanation.definitionFit: Sopranos sing the highest voice part, so they are the women at the top of the vocal range.

clue.text: Use snare to catch tailless spaniel

indicators.note: tailless means the dog's name loses its final letter

parts.note: a springer is a breed of spaniel

explanation.surface: Set a trap to catch a spaniel with no tail.
explanation.definitionFit: A springe is a noose snare for birds or small game, and as a verb it means to catch with one.

clue.text: Type of record broken by fastest runner

definitions.meaning: a recording medium such as cassette or magnetic strip
the finishing line that the race winner breasts

explanation.definitionFit: Recordings are made on magnetic strips, and the winner of a race breaks the strip across the finish line.

clue.text: Distinguished Londoner's parental guidance, guarding young family

indicators.note: guarding means the two letters stand either side of what follows, protecting it

parts.note: PG is the film certificate for parental guidance
early can mean at an immature stage, as in early years
kin are one's relatives

explanation.surface: A notable Londoner's advice as a parent, protecting the children.
explanation.walkthrough: A PEARLY KING is a London costermongers' figure in a suit covered in pearl buttons, collecting for charity.
explanation.definitionFit: This traditional London figure is distinguished in the literal sense, standing out in a suit covered with pearl buttons.

clue.text: Gather around new rebuilt fire

indicators.note: around means the rearranged letters sit either side of the abbreviation
rebuilt says the letters of the word are put together in a new order

explanation.surface: People gather round a freshly relit bonfire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rebuilt' turns FIRE into IFER; 'around' puts it round N.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather can mean to conclude from evidence, which is to infer.

clue.text: A novel such as Madame Bovary

definitions.meaning: Jane Austen's novel about a matchmaking heroine
Flaubert's heroine Madame Bovary has this as her first name

explanation.definitionFit: It is the title of Jane Austen's novel and the first name of Flaubert's heroine Madame Bovary.

clue.text: Saintly Irishman stopped short by Scot from America

indicators.note: stopped short means the saint's name loses its final letter

parts.note: St Columba was an Irish monk who brought Christianity to Scotland
Ian is a typically Scottish first name

explanation.surface: An Irish saint is interrupted by a Scotsman from across the Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stopped short' cuts the last A from COLUMBA, leaving COLUMB.
explanation.definitionFit: Columbia is a poetic name for America, so Columbian means American.

clue.text: Prisoner that's never outgoing?

parts.note: outgoing read literally: a convict serving a whole-life sentence never goes out

explanation.definitionFit: Someone sentenced to imprisonment for life is a convict who may never be released.

clue.text: Miranda's novel utterance

parts.note: words spoken by Miranda in Shakespeare's The Tempest, later the title of Huxley's novel

explanation.walkthrough: In The Tempest, Miranda, who has seen few people, exclaims 'O brave new world, that has such people in't'; Aldous Huxley took the phrase as a novel's title.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both Miranda's exclamation in The Tempest and the title of Aldous Huxley's dystopian novel.
